I think that we are happier here than they can ever be within their walls. No matter how high they are, and how bright their towers shimmer in the summer sun, I like to think that here, in the shadow of the walls of the City which stretches above us, there will always be a primal joy in our faces that they can never hope to rival.

Today is Thanksgiving – the one holiday of our tribe. Just this morning, Elder Sheba was making her rounds around town, garbed in the ceremonial red furs. She entered my house first, and we were sitting on the soil cross legged in a circle, and she joined us on the ground, and she chanted her prayers until my eyes began to close and when I opened them again I was not in my hut but kneeling before a shrine in a forest. An ancient ritual, from a simpler time.

But now, it is noon, and the sundial in our village square casts no shadow upon the ground. An official has arrived from the City, and he is now walking with Elder Sheba. His face is long and his nose is sharp; and he is surveying the walls around him with an amused sharpness. He reminds me of a sparrowhawk, but unlike one he has no wings; he has arrived here in a sleek metal machine which bellows and roars with a ferocity that scares even my people. We do not like him.

If he has left it nearby, I think, its glittering silver paint will be scratched and dented by nightfall, and I will be happy. The beasts here are not gentle ones, they have claws and beaks and worse things besides; things I would not want to meet in the forest past midnight.

And yes, I walk to the edge to town and it is there, a tiny speck in the distance from our village. I think to myself, the bonfire starts at six, and there is time left, time enough for a visit to this metal monument.

I take off my wooden shoes, and then I start to sprint across the plains, barefoot and free, the way I did when I was young. But I go further out this time, to where the machine waits for me, and I think that it looks almost like the City behind me, something huge and vast and metal in the middle of something huger and vaster and greater.

I pace around it, and I see that its door lies open, and my mind tells me not to go in. But it is just too inviting, that cavernous mouth reminding me of the caves in the mountains, where I spent much of my childhood in, listening to the water drip, slowly but surely forming the stalagmites and the stalactites, I cannot remember which are the ones on the ceiling and which are the ones on the floor. I think to myself that perhaps we aren’t too unlike after all.

As soon as I place my first footfall, the memory comes back to me unbidden. Elder Sheba told me once that this beast before me was called a plane. She said that it was a manifestation of their evil and their greed. She reasoned that man was born with legs for a reason, and it was not to fly. Who were we, she asked, to go against our Creator? She, after all, was the one who had given us the forests and the rivers, and it was She who we were thanking on this very day. At that time, I had believed her to the bottom of my heart. But now, I wasn’t so sure. Isn’t it logical for man to want to fly? To see with their own eyes what was beyond the sapphire oceans around their lands? I knew of insects too, which hid in the feathers of birds, using them to get from tree to tree, which otherwise would have taken their tiny legs years upon years.

Steel and earth. Were they really so different?

There is something on the wall, with numbers on it. I look at it, then at the sky, then back at it again. It seems to tell the time. And if it is true, and it is, the dance nears, and like the wind I must run. And so I do, back through the knee length grass, back to my home, back to the assortment of huts by the river, back into the shadow of the looming City.

I arrive just in time for the dance, and the first thing I see are the flames, licking at the ends of the logs. I can taste the woodsmoke in the air, sweet and bitter at the same time. I hear the beat of the war drums around me, and I twirl my body to their rhythm, going ever faster as their pounding grows ever louder within my ears. My hand brushes against something, it is smooth, and when I turn around to look, it is the arm of the emissary from the City. There is a frenzied look in his eyes, and something wild and primal in the smile that stretches across his face. I breathe in now, and mixed with the woodsmoke there is something fragrant coming from his body, a fresh minty tang which reminds me of the forests and the plains.
